blocks.content: Weathering, erosion, and deposition are powerful exogenic processes that continuously shape and reshape the Earth’s surface. These processes act over millions of years and are responsible for the formation of soils, valleys, plains, deserts, coastal features, and glacial landscapes. For SSC examinations, this chapter is very important because questions are frequently asked on types of weathering, agents of erosion, specific landforms formed by rivers, wind, glaciers, and sea waves.
PART A: WEATHERING

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Weathering is an in situ process of disintegration and decomposition of rocks without any movement of material.
Mechanical weathering dominates in cold and dry regions, whereas chemical weathering is most effective in hot and humid climates.
Erosion involves the removal, transportation, and reshaping of material by rivers, wind, glaciers, and sea waves.
Rivers carve out V-shaped valleys during erosion, while glaciers create U-shaped valleys.
Deposition occurs when a transporting agent loses energy, forming features like deltas, sand dunes, moraines, and beaches.

blocks.content: Meaning of Weathering

Weathering is the process of disintegration and decomposition of rocks in situ, that is, at the place where rocks are found, without any movement of material. Weathering weakens rocks and prepares them for erosion. It is the first stage in the process of landform development.
Types of Weathering
Mechanical (Physical) Weathering

Mechanical weathering involves the physical breaking of rocks into smaller fragments without changing their chemical composition. It is dominant in cold and dry regions or areas with extreme temperature variations.
Important processes include exfoliation due to expansion and contraction, frost action where water freezes and expands in cracks, and pressure release caused by removal of overlying rock layers.
Chemical Weathering
Chemical weathering involves chemical alteration of rocks through reactions with water, oxygen, carbon dioxide, and acids. It is most effective in hot and humid climates.
Major chemical processes include oxidation (rusting of iron), carbonation (reaction with carbonic acid), hydration (absorption of water), and solution (dissolving of minerals).
Biological Weathering

Biological weathering is caused by plants, animals, and human activities. Plant roots penetrate cracks and widen them, burrowing animals loosen soil, and human activities such as mining and construction accelerate weathering.
PART B: EROSION AND LANDFORMS
Meaning of Erosion
Erosion is the process of removal, transportation, and reshaping of weathered material by natural agents such as rivers, wind, glaciers, and sea waves.
Agents of Erosion and Their Landforms
River (Running Water) Erosion Landforms
Weathering is the process of disintegration and decomposition of rocks in situ, that is, at the place where rocks are found, without any movement of material.
Rivers are the most important agents of erosion. They erode land through hydraulic action, abrasion, attrition, and solution.
Major erosional landforms created by rivers include V-shaped valleys, interlocking spurs, gorges, canyons, waterfalls, potholes, and river cliffs.
Wind Erosion Landforms
Wind is an important agent of erosion in arid and semi-arid regions. Wind erodes land mainly through deflation and abrasion.
Erosional landforms formed by wind include mushroom rocks, yardangs, deflation hollows, and rock pedestals.
Glacial Erosion Landforms
Glaciers erode land by plucking and abrasion. They are powerful agents of erosion in cold regions.
Glacial erosional landforms include U-shaped valleys, cirques, arêtes, horns, hanging valleys, and fjords.
Marine Erosion Landforms
Sea waves erode coastlines through hydraulic action, abrasion, and corrosion.

blocks.content: Marine erosional landforms include sea cliffs, sea caves, sea arches, stacks, and wave-cut platforms.
PART C: DEPOSITION AND LANDFORMS
Meaning of Deposition
Deposition is the process by which transported material is laid down when the transporting agent loses energy.
Depositional Landforms by Different Agents
River Depositional Landforms
Rivers deposit sediments mainly in their middle and lower courses.
Important river depositional landforms include floodplains, natural levees, meanders, oxbow lakes, deltas, and alluvial plains.
Wind Depositional Landforms
Wind deposits sand and dust particles in deserts and semi-arid regions.
Wind depositional landforms include sand dunes (barchans, longitudinal, transverse), and loess plains.
Glacial Depositional Landforms
Glaciers deposit unsorted material known as till.

items: Weathering occurs strictly in situ (no movement), whereas erosion requires removal and transport of materials.
V-shaped valleys are formed by river erosion, whereas U-shaped valleys are carved by glacial erosion.
Mushroom rocks and yardangs are wind erosional landforms, while barchans and loess are wind depositional landforms.
Glaciers deposit unsorted material known as till, which forms moraines, drumlins, and eskers.

blocks.content: Glacial depositional landforms include moraines (lateral, medial, terminal), eskers, drumlins, and outwash plains.
Marine Depositional Landforms
Sea waves deposit sediments along coastlines.
Marine depositional landforms include beaches, spits, bars, tombolos, and lagoons.
Importance of Weathering, Erosion & Deposition

These processes are responsible for soil formation, development of fertile plains, shaping of landforms, and availability of resources. They play a crucial role in agriculture, settlement, transport, and overall human life.
